Project homeResults summary

What earlier work predicts for our expression data

Heat did not slow healing, but it stopped most wounded fragments from forming radial corallites. Earlier Acropora studies suggest the expression data can tell us why: look at skeleton-building genes 10 days after wounding.

RNA-seq from our long-term heating (LTH) experiment, sampled at days 1, 3 and 10. Updated 19 November 2026.

Two ways the day 10 data could look

Sketches of expected patterns, not data.

Heat also cut growth in unwounded fragments (10.2% vs 16.0%), so the test is whether the lines diverge, not whether 31 °C sits lower.

Our samples against earlier timelines

Our day 10 sample falls before radial corallites form and inside the second wave of wound genes seen in A. aspera. Han's skeleton genes peaked later, in a slower species.

What each gene set should do

Gene setDay 1Day 10
Early wound responsec-Fos, c-Jun, JNK and ERK kinases, Toll-like receptors, NF-κB, TRAF6, lectins, complementWounded differ from unwounded at both temperatures. Heat changed this little in A. aspera; c-Jun rose more under heat.A second rise is possible: c-Fos, ERK2 and TRAF6 rose again at day 10 in A. aspera.
Skeleton buildingGalaxin 2, Saarp2, mucin, Usomp, carbonic anhydrase 2, collagens, calicoblast markersLittle change yet. These genes rose in mid-to-late regrowth in A. muricata.The key test. If heat blocks regrowth, wounding raises these genes less at 31 °C than at 28 °C.
Heat stress and energyRibosomal and mitochondrial genes, antioxidant genes, heat shock proteinsDiffer between temperatures in wounded and unwounded fragments alike.Same. Chronic 32 °C did not raise HSP70 or HSP90 in A. aspera, so expect a weak heat shock signal.

Before reading too much into a result

  • Heat also cut growth in unwounded fragments (10.2% vs 16.0%), so heated versus ambient wounded fragments alone cannot show that heat blocks regrowth.
  • Heated fragments lost most of their symbionts. Fewer symbiont-hosting cells can shift host expression without any gene changing its regulation, so check key results against each sample's symbiont density.
  • Our D1 sample (24 h) may miss the earliest wound peak, which came at 6 h in A. millepora.
  • The skeleton-building genes come from one single-cell study at day 21 in a slower-regenerating species.
  • Fluorescent protein results in the wounding studies are protein, not RNA, so they do not predict our data.

Sources

  • Xu et al. 2023 A. millepora, aquaria, 6 h to 10 days. Wnt, FGF, ADAMTS, galaxin and c-Fos peak 6 h after wounding.
  • van de Water et al. 2015a A. aspera, on the reef, 16 h to 10 days. Immune genes respond in waves; c-Fos rises at days 4 and 10; c-Jun never changes.
  • van de Water et al. 2015b A. aspera, heat then wounding, 24 h. Heat changes the wound response little; c-Jun rises more under heat. Two aquaria per temperature.
  • Bonesso et al. 2017 A. aspera, tips removed, 26 vs 32 °C, 12 days. Heat halves tip regrowth; HSP70 and HSP90 do not rise.
  • Han et al. 2025 A. muricata, tips cut, to 39 days; single cells at day 21. Skeleton-building genes rise in mid-to-late regrowth, which peaks at days 15–27.
